Derived from marketplace_test_bank.json's journey lane by tools/build_live_mcp_registry.py - do not hand-edit the rows, edit the CATEGORIES table and regenerate. `status` moves owed -> walked -> green as the flywheel turns; findings accumulate per scenario so a re-walk can prove a fix rather than re-discover it.

categories.A-discovery: can a stranger FIND the thing they came for? (40% of simulated journey failures died here)
categories.B-listing-lifecycle: can a seller get a listing from nothing to live, and know why when they cannot?
categories.C-inquiry: can a buyer reach a human, and does the seller learn about it?
categories.D-service-hail: can a client raise a job and a provider take it, both knowing what state it is in?
categories.E-money: at the moment money moves, does every screen agree on the number?
categories.F-credits: does a person understand what credits are, what they hold, and what they will get back?
categories.G-trust: is a trust signal earned, visible, and impossible to mint for yourself?
categories.H-moderation: can an admin act, and is a non-admin visibly refused rather than silently ignored?
categories.I-map: does the map tell the truth about where someone is, and stay quiet when it should not?
categories.J-degraded: offline, slow, or failing: does the product REFUSE OUT LOUD instead of pretending?
categories.K-a11y: keyboard, screen reader, contrast, focus order - can this be used without a mouse or good eyes?
categories.L-comprehension: is the wording readable, translated, and free of jargon at the moment it costs money?
categories.M-mobile: at 390 CSS pixels, is every control reachable and every target big enough?
categories.N-continuity: does the page hold its shape while data arrives, and survive a reload mid-flow?
categories.O-empty-error: does an empty state promise only what the product can deliver?
categories.Q-payment-rails: THREE GCash accounts meet here - the buyer's, the provider's, and the founder's personal 0995 009 2416 - and only one of them may ever be on a given screen. WorkHive has no business registration and therefore no merchant account, so every rail is a personal number: a buyer pays the PROVIDER directly and the platform never touches it, while a provider tops up credits by paying the FOUNDER. Put the founder's number on a buyer's payment step and the buyer sends job money to someone who is not party to the job, cannot fulfil it, and cannot reconcile it - and nothing errors. This is also the friction Ian named by hand: 'hassle free ... like the hassle of payment two gcash accounts'. A buyer must see exactly ONE number.
categories.P-isolation: can one tenant see or touch another's rows, through any screen?
categories.S-adversarial: when a guard refuses someone, does the SCREEN teach them why - or just go quiet? The 500 simulations proved the economics hold; none of them looked at a page
categories.T-two-context: buyer and provider signed in AT THE SAME TIME, acting on one job. Every walk so far has been one identity at a time, so races, stale views and 'who sees the state change first' are invisible by construction
categories.U-recovery: the flywheel has walked STEADY states; almost every money defect this session lived in a TRANSITION - reload mid-flow, Back out of a sheet, a session that expires between typing an amount and pressing Confirm
categories.V-edge-content: boundary rendering, where truncation and overflow hide: the longest title, a zero price, 200% zoom, a 50-listing seller, a name in a non-Latin script
categories.W-surface-breadth: a marketplace user does not stop at the marketplace. Four categories touch only six surfaces; these are the pages a real journey reaches next and no walk has ever opened
categories.R-money-lifecycle: does a peso that enters this system arrive where the ledger says it does, on EVERY branch?

personas.spammer: floods listings to occupy the grid - capped at 3 live until one sells, plus a 2%/month holding fee; the question is whether the cap explains itself
personas.sybil: farms starter grants across fresh accounts - only ID verification touches this, so the screen must not imply a remedy that does not exist
personas.scam_provider: takes the job and the direct peso payment, never delivers. The platform holds no money and CANNOT claw it back - the completion window is the only lever
personas.scam_buyer: receives the work then objects in bad faith to avoid settling
personas.colluder: a paired account trading credits with itself to extract value - structurally impossible (every leg is a transfer, credits are non-withdrawable), so the oracle is EXACTLY 0 extracted, proven not assumed

findings.title: the credits-back chip reads PHP500 on EVERY priced listing, so it stops informing
findings.measured: 9 of 18 cards carry a price; all 9 are PHP20,309-PHP236,110 and every chip reads PHP500.00. Each one AGREES with listing_reservation_amount() -- the per-listing cap is binding exactly as designed.
findings.why_it_matters: The cap was chosen from simulation for the PROVIDER side: it measured 4.9x throughput at scale, because a flat 10% locks PHP2,500 on a PHP25,000 listing and exhausts the supply. Nobody measured what it does to the BUYER side. On this catalogue the headline promise -- 10% back -- is worth 2.5% on the cheapest visible listing and 0.2% on the dearest, and the chip shows an identical number on both, so it can no longer help anyone choose.
findings.not_a_bug: The arithmetic is right and the guard is right. This is a DESIGN tension the simulation could not see, because it modelled provider throughput and not buyer comprehension.
options: state the RATE next to the amount ('PHP500 back - 0.2%'), so the cap is visible rather than disguised
raise reward_max_per_listing for industrial sections, where the current cap rounds the reward to noise
show the chip only when the reward is a meaningful fraction, and say nothing when it is not
findings.next: put this to Ian as an economy decision; do not silently change a simulated knob

findings.title: the filtered-empty state told people to 'clear the filters' and gave them nothing to press
findings.measured: Searching a term that matches nothing rendered 'No listings match those filters. Try a different search term or category, or clear the filters...' with ZERO buttons or links inside the grid. The only clear-ish control on the page was the 'All' category chip, measured 1,020px below the message, and it resets the CATEGORY while leaving the search term in place.
findings.why_it_matters: Discovery is 40% of simulated journey failures. This is the moment a stranger who mistyped decides whether the catalogue is empty or they made a mistake - and the single instruction on screen was not performable from where they were standing.
findings.fix: A 'Clear filters' button inside the empty state, delegated on document (the empty state re-renders on every load, so a boot-time binding would attach to a node that does not exist yet). Resets BOTH halves - category AND search term - because the message says 'the filters', and clearing half of what you promise is the same broken promise in a smaller box. Returns focus to the search box.
findings.verified_live: search 'zzzznothingmatchesthis' -> '' · cards 0 -> 9 · active chip -> 'All' · URL query cleared · focus back on #search-input · button 93x44px
findings.also_checked: Suspected the message sat below the fold; measured 341px between the search box and the message, so it is visible from where they typed. Not a fold problem - checked rather than assumed.

findings.title: the account gate explained itself and then stranded the person
findings.measured: anon opens a PHP68,980 listing -> Contact Seller -> redirected to index.html?signin=1. The gate DOES toast a good reason ('Contacting a seller needs a WorkHive account, so they know who is asking. Joining is free.'), but nothing was stored: no ?return=, no wh_return_to, and index.html had no return handling at all. After signing in they landed on the homepage's marketing copy and had to find the listing again from scratch.
findings.why_it_matters: Discovery is 40% of simulated journey failures. This threw away the one visitor who had already survived discovery AND formed intent - the most expensive person on the site to lose.
findings.fix: marketplace stores the destination in sessionStorage before redirecting; index.html honours it after sign-in, scoped to same-origin /workhive/ paths because a destination read from storage is still untrusted input and an open redirect is how that becomes a phishing hop.
findings.second_half: The destination was only ever 'the marketplace', because the detail is a SHEET and opening one never changed the URL - a listing could not be shared, bookmarked or returned to at all. openDetailSheet now writes ?listing=<id> (replaceState, so Back still leaves the page), closeSheet drops it, and boot honours it after the listings arrive.
findings.verified_live: gate stores /workhive/marketplace.html?listing=<id>; a cold load of that URL opens the Honeywell listing; closing clears the param. 18/18 marketplace journey + discovery specs green.
findings.instrument_notes: Two false readings caught: querySelector('[role=dialog],.modal') returned the first CLOSED overlay rather than the open sheet, and the toast probe matched the provenance chip because it carries role=status. Scoped to .sheet.open and read the source instead.

findings.title: three KPI tiles rendered a raw auth error where the explanation belongs
findings.measured: live: '- ACTIVE TODAY / JWT issued at future', same for AI SPEND TODAY and ACTIVE HIVES. Five 401s in the console; the reads themselves were fine when retried, so it is a startup race (clock skew puts the JWT's iat in the future), not a permission problem.
findings.why_it_matters: The dash was RIGHT - the Calm Dashboard contract says show the gap, never fiction. What sat beside it was internal plumbing: 'JWT issued at future' tells a founder nothing and reads as a broken tile. And it was general - ANY read failure would have leaked its raw message.
findings.fix: statGapReason() maps the failure shape to something a person can act on (sign-in still settling / no connection / not permitted / unavailable), keeps the value as an honest '-', and preserves the raw text in a title for debugging.
findings.verified: the tiles SUCCEEDED on the verification load, so the error path did not run on its own - exercised directly instead: all four shapes translate, the sub reads 'sign-in still settling - reload', the title still holds 'JWT issued at future', and the value stays '-'.

findings.title: a signed-out stranger sees numbers that match the database, and no credit promise they cannot act on
findings.measured: Walked TRULY anonymous - signOut + cleared every wh_* key + RELOADED, because clearing keys without a reload leaves the prior signed-in DOM up and contaminates the read. Verified no session before measuring. Every tab badge matches its section: Parts 9 / Training 6 / Services 0 against published parts=9, training=6, services=0. The grid rendered exactly 9 children and the footer said 'Showing 9 listings · newest first. Sellers cannot pay for placement.' - a disclosure that is both true and the kind a marketplace usually omits.
findings.note: An apparent 9-vs-21 mismatch was MY instrument: the page's total published is 21, split jobs=6 / parts=9 / training=6, and my first probe guessed three section names and missed 'jobs'. The page under-renders nothing. Also observed and NOT filed as a defect: anon sees zero credit copy. Credits are a signed-in concept and the page promises the stranger nothing it cannot keep - though the 10%-back earn line is arguably a selling point worth showing signed-out. That is a product call for Ian, not a correctness bug.

findings.title: an anonymous visitor could TRUNCATE 140 tables - RLS is never consulted for TRUNCATE
findings.measured: as anon, rolled back: `truncate table public.marketplace_sellers cascade` SUCCEEDED, table read 0 rows. 140 tables anon-truncatable, 142 for authenticated, ~104,000 rows.
findings.why_gates_missed_it: validate_unprotected_write_grant requires RLS behind any write grant - correct for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, INERT for TRUNCATE. marketplace_sellers has RLS on and passed cleanly.
findings.fix: mig 20260803000028 revokes schema-wide + ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES; gate `no-client-truncate` locks it. storage.* TRACKED (postgres is not superuser and cannot assume supabase_storage_admin) and printed every run.

findings.title: browser_resize(390) yields innerWidth 585 - every M-mobile scenario walked via MCP is a FALSE reading
findings.measured: browser_resize(390x844) then echoing innerWidth returned 585. A tap-target sweep at that width reported 0 violations, which says nothing about 390.
findings.why_it_matters: M-mobile is 12 of the 197 scenarios and its whole question is 'at 390 CSS pixels'. Walking them through an instrument that silently renders 585 would bank 12 green cells for a viewport nobody uses - the most expensive kind of pass, because it retires the question.
findings.resolution: M-mobile scenarios are walked through the PLAYWRIGHT SPEC lane (node node_modules/@playwright/test/cli.js), which sets the viewport deterministically - the marketplace-sim specs already assert 44px targets at a real 390. MCP keeps the categories where it is sound: content, wiring, oracles, a11y tree, and cross-persona reachability.
findings.rule: ECHO THE VIEWPORT INSIDE THE PAGE before trusting any width-dependent measurement.

findings.title: a FAILED services read told the buyer they had no jobs
findings.measured: Forced the services read to reject and re-ran loadClientServices. The pane rendered the FIRST-RUN INVITATION -- 'No requests yet. Hail your first service below - a nearby provider accepts and you track them here.' saysError false, showsFirstRunInvite true. findings.why_it_matters: supabase-js does NOT throw on a query error; it resolves with { data: null, error }. So `catRes.data || []` and `mineRes.data || []` turned every failure into an empty array and the renderer painted the empty state. Telling someone they have no jobs when we simply could not look is worse than saying nothing: a buyer with a job in flight is told it does not exist, and the invitation actively encourages them to hail a SECOND provider for work already under way.
findings.fix: Check catRes.error / mineRes.error explicitly and throw, so the existing catch renders the honest state. Same defect the listings grid already fixed as P7 on 2026-07-24 ('load-failure rendered the first-run be-the-first-to-sell CTA'); the services pane was never swept for it.
findings.teeth: With the read forced to fail: "Couldn't load services / TypeError: probe: forced network failure / Retry" -- saysError true, offersRetry true, stillInvites FALSE. With the read restored: the pane renders the buyer's 3 real requests, no error. An empty result and a failed read are now different facts on this surface.

findings.title: a provider is blocked from listing by a commission the platform has REPEALED
findings.measured: service_knob_pct(commission_pct) is now 0.00 -- the plan's decision landed. But three historical commission rows totalling -PHP360 remain, and Pablo Aguilar Mechanical Works sits at exactly -200.00 from a single entry: 'commission -200.00 | 5% commission - Laser Shaft Alignment PHP4,000 | 2026-07-28'. The seller surface tells them 'Negative balance: top up to keep accepting jobs.' So they must send real pesos to clear a charge levied under a rule the platform has since renounced.
findings.why_it_matters: The plan says two things that now pull against each other: 'No revenue. The platform takes no commission' and 'History is never rewritten: existing commission entries stay.' Both were right when written. The live consequence nobody had looked at is that the platform is still holding PHP360 taken under the repealed rule, and at least one provider is blocked from listing until they replace it.
findings.options: (1) Leave it: the charge was valid when made and history stands. (2) Reverse it with COMPENSATING entries -- append-only, no history rewritten, exactly how apply_dispute_adjustment already undoes money -- which returns the PHP360 and unblocks the provider without deleting a single row. Option 2 is consistent with both plan rules simultaneously; it is a five-line migration. IAN'S CALL: this is his money, not a defect I should decide.

findings.measured: Canonical parity walked in-browser through the page's OWN client, so the comparison runs against the same database and the same RLS the page sees -- not a side-channel psql query, which would be a different reader answering a different question. Eight figures, eight exact matches: top-ups badge 1 / rows 1 vs v_service_credit_topups_truth pending=1; listings 3 / 3 vs draft=3; sellers 9 / 9 vs unverified=9; feedback 10 / 10 vs platform_feedback waiting (new+triaged+in_progress)=10. The feedback badge deliberately counts WAITING rather than total, and the DB query was written to match that definition -- a badge that counted everything would have read 10 here too, by coincidence, and hidden the difference.

findings.title: three more readers still split one person's wallet in two -- and it made EVERY credit payment impossible
findings.measured: mig 39 unified the wallet for three readers and missed three: guard_reward_spend_cap (the balance check behind every credit payment), my_credit_balance() (what the buyer's own confirm sheet reads), and apply_dispute_adjustment (the bound on what an adjudication recovers). Measured live: every credit in this economy sits in the PROVIDER namespace -- three provider accounts hold it, there is not one consumer row. On an 800 job (10% cap 80) with the person holding 340: 'the guard SEES 0' and spending 80 was REFUSED 23514 'Not enough credits: balance is PHP0, this would spend PHP80.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is not an edge case, it is the whole feature. With all credits provider-side, NO buyer could spend credits at all -- the spend half of the earn-or-spend switch had never been able to fire. And the refusal takes the cruellest shape a money error can: it tells someone holding PHP340 that their balance is zero. my_credit_balance() is the same bug one layer up, so the sheet offered no spend field and the buyer never even reached the refusal -- screen and guard agreed, and both were wrong. apply_dispute_adjustment is quieter but costs real money: it under-reads what a provider still holds, so the difference is silently booked as a shortfall the PLATFORM absorbs while the provider keeps credits the adjudication said to return.
findings.fix: mig 20260803000041 repoints all three at person_credit_balance(). No ledger row moves -- the ledger is append-only and its history is correct; only the readers change, exactly as mig 39 did. A namespace may go negative while the PERSON stays positive: a namespace is a bookkeeping location, not a wallet.
findings.teeth: A: the refused spend now ACCEPTED, person 340 -> 260. B: one peso over the 10% cap still REFUSED 23514. C: a person holding 0 across BOTH namespaces still REFUSED 23514. my_credit_balance() as the signed-in buyer returns 340.00 (was 0). findings.title: the 10,000,000 supply cap did not watch the only door credits actually use
findings.measured: issue_credits() is the ceiling -- it takes authorised - issued FOR UPDATE, refuses when the remainder is too small, and increments issued_credits. Exactly ONE function called it: claim_starter_grant. The other mint, in guard_service_topup_status on every verified GCash top-up, inserted its ledger row directly and never touched the treasury. Live: credit_treasury issued = 0.00 while the ledger held topup = 1,500.00 across 2 rows (starter_grant = 0 rows). Every credit that exists came through the door nobody was counting.
findings.why_it_matters: Two consequences. (1) The cap was UNENFORCED on the primary mint path: issued_credits never grew, so authorised - issued was always the full 10,000,000 and no top-up could ever be refused for exhausting supply -- the ceiling that 'guarantees every credit in circulation is honourable' guarded a door credits do not use. (2) The founder console reads authorised_credits and issued_credits from v_credit_posture to state the platform's own position, and showed 0 issued while PHP1,500 circulated. A money figure that is confidently wrong is worse than one that is missing.
findings.fix: mig 20260803000042: the top-up mint now issues against the ceiling, exactly as the starter grant does, BEFORE the ledger insert -- so a refusal aborts the statement and the refusal and the mint can never disagree. issued_credits back-filled from the ledger (0.00 -> 1,500.00); a counter corrected to match the rows it summarises is not a history rewrite, and the append-only ledger was untouched. The migration RAISES if the two still disagree afterwards.
findings.teeth: A: verifying a PHP500 top-up with only PHP100 unissued was REFUSED 23514, 0 ledger rows written, and the status stayed pending_verification so the founder can retry after a governance decision. B: a PHP100 top-up against exactly PHP100 remaining MINTED and drove remaining to 0.00. Screen half, walked live in platform-actions: the toast read the guard's own sentence verbatim -- 'Only 100 credits remain unissued; cannot issue 500. The supply is capped at 10,000,000 and that ceiling is what guarantees every credit in circulation is honourable.' -- not the generic 'Action failed. Try again.' All four credit gates green afterwards.

findings.measured: Two jobs staged completed 10 days ago, both past the 3-day objection deadline. The buyer objected to one: raise_service_objection returned {ok:true}, the job moved completed -> disputed, and the reason was journalled to service_job_events ('buyer raised a problem inside the objection window: The unit still leaks after the visit'). The control's payment carries auto_confirmed_at set and confirmed_by NULL, so an auto-settlement is never recorded as a person attesting to the amount. A second sweep in the same transaction returned {settled: 0} -- idempotent.

findings.note: THE PROBE'S OWN THREE BUGS ARE WHY IT IS TRUSTWORTHY, and each is a banked class. (1) It read only stdout while every verdict line is a psql NOTICE on stderr -- all four reported 'no verdict line', a false red.
